title: The Nanaksar tradition
hook: a tradition of continuous kirtan and reading begun by Baba Nand Singh

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akhand Kirtani Jatha, the company of unbroken singing. Your line was kirtan till dawn. Was there a song in the last sound you heard last night? Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

A relay race only works if the baton never touches the ground. One runner tires, and another is already moving alongside, hand out. Now set that race indoors, slow it down, and make the baton a voice. One reader finishes a stretch of the Guru Granth Sahib, and another is already seated, ready to go on without a gap. Down the hall, a small group sings, and when they rest, another group takes up the hymn. That is the picture at a Nanaksar gurdwara: the praise doesn't stop when one person does. Today's stream is built on that.
screen: `A BATON THAT NEVER TOUCHES THE GROUND.` → `ONE READER HANDS ON TO THE NEXT.` → `THE PRAISE DOESN'T STOP.`

segments.voice: The Nanaksar tradition grew around Baba Nand Singh, a holy man remembered in Sikh tradition for long stretches of solitary meditation and for a deep, almost personal reverence for the Guru Granth Sahib. His followers carried on what he began, and Nanaksar centers keep it going today. Three things stand out. First, continuous praise. At Nanaksar centers, reading of the Granth and singing of kirtan are kept going in turns, so that the Guru's word is always sounding somewhere in the house. Second, the Granth treated as a living Guru in very concrete ways. Tradition at Nanaksar is known for care like that given to an honored person: food prepared and offered with great attention, the Granth's resting place kept with tenderness. The Granth is Guru for the whole panth; Nanaksar is known for making that honor detailed and constant. Third, simplicity of life for those who lead. Tradition remembers the babas of Nanaksar as renunciants who asked little for themselves. Where does continuous praise come from? Open the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's long hymn of peace, on Ang 262. Its first stanza opens, in paraphrase: remember, remember, keep remembering, and find peace. The repetition is the teaching. The word for remembering, simran, isn't a single act; the hymn says it over and over, as if to show it should never quite stop. A Nanaksar center turns that line into the shape of a building: some voice, always, keeping the remembering going. Sikhs hold different views about some Nanaksar customs, and their place beside the common code is discussed. The aim itself is plain: a house where the praise doesn't fall silent.
screen: `BABA NAND SINGH: MEDITATION AND REVERENCE.` · `READING AND KIRTAN KEPT GOING IN TURNS.` · `THE GRANTH HONORED AS A LIVING GURU.` · `ANG 262: REMEMBER, KEEP REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `CONTINUOUS PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to kirtan quietly. Play a recording of Gurbani kirtan if one is at hand, low enough that you have to lean in a little. If you don't, listen to the quietest sound in the room. Let it run without you doing anything to it. When your attention drifts off, just come back, the way one reader hands on to the next. Each return is a fresh start, not a failure. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru as you return. The bell holds the time.
The Nanaksar tradition. A Sikh stream that grew around Baba Nand Singh, known for keeping reading and kirtan going in turns, and for detailed reverence for the Granth as a living Guru. Today's word.

Your line: continuous praise. Today, pick one small thing to keep going in turns with someone else: a playlist, a thank-you thread, a shared chore. Notice what changes when it never stops with you. Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

options: the room waits in silence until morning.
